prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved from B003 to B024 as my single preferred part, and I want to say plainly why. In round 1 my argument for moire graphene was the pattern I value most: a specific prediction, then a clue from nature, then wide replication. I still value it. But the exchange showed me that the pattern is only half of what the committee needs, the other half being a discovery whose central finding is settled and whose credit can be written down honestly. Optical lattice clocks meet both. Katori's magic-wavelength condition is a concrete idea that removes the trap-induced shift, the first strontium lattice clock realised it, and the record accuracy of Ye's group at the 10^-18 level has been reproduced independently at RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE. Kroll persuaded me on the comb: the comb is a ruler for optical frequencies, whereas the lattice clock is a different invention that needs the magic condition, many-atom interrogation and years of systematics work, and the 2005 and 2012 citations did not anticipate it. What the clocks give is a new capability that already touches nature: gravitational redshift across millimetres, limits on drifting constants, dark-matter searches and many-body physics inside the clock. That is a discovery-driven reason to honour it, not only a metrological one. Every file that discusses it names the same two people, which is rare on this shortlist. I would word the citation on what has been demonstrated, the invention and the 10^-18 realisation, and not lean on the redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: I do not retreat from my old worry that this is a quantitative leap in an existing field and not a new phenomenon, and Johansson, Lindroth and Kroll all list the same overlap with 2005 and 2012 as their own main reservation. Two credit questions remain open to me. First, whether Ye's contribution to the record accuracy is invention or excellent systematic-control engineering built on Katori's concept, as Kroll asks. Second, whether the first lattice-clock demonstrations by Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley are fairly covered by two names; I cannot verify priority dates from the materials in front of me, and Olsson is right that the historical record should be checked. If the committee instead wants a new regime of matter, B003 remains a serious candidate, and my reservations about it (the unresolved pairing mechanism, the missing Cao, the limit of three names) are about timing, not about whether the physics is real.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is not a refinement of the 2005 comb prize or the 2012 ion-control prize: it needs the magic-wavelength condition, many-atom interrogation and years of work on systematics, and the clocks already meet the criteria for redefining the second, so there is no reason to wait. He also says the pairing mechanism in B003 is unsettled and wants more consolidation.
responses.response: You moved me on the overlap. In round 1 I rated the comb and ion-control prizes as a reason for caution; your point that the comb is only a readout ruler and that the neutral-atom lattice is a separate idea is the distinction the citation should draw, and I will support wording that says so. I also accept that we should not make the prize depend on the formal redefinition. Where I stay a little apart is the kind of result. You call it a technique that changes what can be observed, and I agree that the geodesy and constant-drift tests show nature answering. I would still like the citation to name the invention and the 10^-18 realisation, and not to claim more novelty than there is. On B003 your experimentalist worry about sample dependence and pairing is fair, and it is part of why I no longer press it this year.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B024 first and B003 third. She says the settled physics and cross-laboratory agreement at 1e-18 should outweigh the theory-then-experiment pattern, that the mechanism and twist-angle disorder in B003 are unresolved, and that a moire prize would be defensible in a few years. She also admits proximity to the field.
responses.response: I now agree with the substance of this. In round 1 I said the open mechanism was a sign of a living field and not a bar, and I still think a prize does not need a mechanism. But you put your finger on what actually decides it for 2026: with the clocks the number is agreed by several laboratories, whereas in twisted graphene the sample dependence, the twist-angle disorder and the pairing question mean the community is still building its picture. Since your proximity to the field is declared, I would ask you and Kroll to tell us plainly what the first-demonstration record shows for Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley. I will take your word on the many-body part as a candidate for the citation, but I would keep it as a consequence, not the headline.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, stresses that the magic angle was predicted and not fitted, and says the citation must say that the discovery is recognised and must not pretend the credit is complete. B024 is his strong second choice.
responses.response: We were together on B003 in round 1, so I owe you an account of why I am leaving. I fully share the weight you give to the specific prediction, and I still think it is the most attractive discovery pattern on the list. Two things moved me. First, the credit: your suggestion that we recognise the group leader and say openly that the credit is incomplete is honest, but it still passes over Cao, the first author, and I would not like to defend that choice in 2026 if we could instead recognise something with a complete two-name attribution. Second, maturity: we both argued that a mechanism is not required, and I still hold that, but in this round no one has said B003 has less need of a few more years than B024, and I cannot say it either. I would be glad if you stay with B003 and register it as a clear alternative for a later year.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B006 (Vicsek, Toner, Ramaswamy) because a minimal model exposes the mechanism and a controlled hydrodynamic theory explains it, and notes that B003's central phenomenon is not understood whereas B006's mechanism is. He admits that quantitative tests of the Toner-Tu exponents are only partial and that Tu is omitted.
responses.response: Your point that B006 has an understood mechanism whereas B003 does not is fair, and it counts for something with me, because I distrust elegant theory without clues from nature. But for the same reason I cannot put B006 first: you yourself say that quantitative tests of the Toner-Tu exponents are only partial, so the theory is stronger than the confirmation, and Tu's omission leaves a real hole in the credit. The chair's question about which experiments measure the exponents quantitatively has not been answered by anyone, including you. If you can name a vibrated-granular or motility-assay measurement of the exponents that is accepted as quantitative, I would reconsider; otherwise it stays below B024 and B003 for me.

uncertainties: Whether the first lattice-clock demonstrations (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) give any of them a claim that a two-name credit would pass over; I cannot settle this from the materials available.
Whether Ye's record-accuracy work is credited as invention or as engineering on top of Katori's concept, which affects the wording of the citation but not the two names.
Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as a distinct discovery after 2005 and 2012, or as a continuation, a point on which Kroll has persuaded me but others may differ.
Whether a two-part prize with B003 could be justified, which would need five names and so exceeds the three-person limit, and I do not propose it.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no specific conflict for the shortlisted candidates: my PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited in any shortlisted ballot, and as far as the provided profile shows none of the credited names is at Uppsala. I note that I changed from B003 to B024 after discussion, not because of any personal connection.
